'''Lacock Abbey''' is a [[country house]] in the village of [[Lacock]], Wiltshire, England. There was an [[Lacock Abbey (monastery)|abbey of nuns]] on the site until 1539, and the house is a remodelling and extension of the abbey's cloister court. The Grade I listed building is owned by the [[National Trust]] and is notable as the site of [[Henry Fox Talbot]]'s pioneering work in photography in the 1830s.

The religious institution was founded in the early 13th century by [[Ela of Salisbury, 3rd Countess of Salisbury|Ela, Countess of Salisbury]], as a [[nunnery]] of the [[Augustinians|Augustinian]] order. The abbey remained a nunnery until the [[dissolution of the monasteries]] in the 16th century; the property was then sold to Sir [[William Sharington]] who converted the convent into a residence where he and his family lived. It was fortified and remained loyal to the crown during the [[English Civil War]], but surrendered to the Parliamentary forces once [[Devizes]] had fallen in 1645.

The house was built over the old cloisters and its main rooms are on the first floor. It is a stone house with stone slated roofs, twisted chimney stacks and [[mullion]]ed windows. Throughout the life of the building, many architectural alterations, additions, and renovations have occurred so that the house is a mish-mash of periods and styles. The Tudor stable courtyard to the north of the house has retained many of its original features including a [[Brewery|brewhouse]] and [[Bakery|bakehouse]].

The house later passed into the hands of the Talbot family, and in 1835 Henry Fox Talbot made what may be the earliest surviving photographic camera negative, an image of one of the windows. In 1944, Matilda Theresa Talbot gave the house and the surrounding village of Lacock to the National Trust. The abbey houses the Fox Talbot Museum.

== History ==
{{For|the history of the abbey until its dissolution|Lacock Abbey (monastery)}}
Lacock Abbey, dedicated to St Mary and St Bernard, was founded in 1232 by Ela, Countess of Salisbury, widow of [[William de Longespee, 3rd Earl of Salisbury|William Longespee]], an illegitimate son of [[Henry II of England|Henry II]].<ref name=":0">The ''Book of Lacock'' mentioned by heralds, passed into the [[Cottonian Library]], where it was apparently lost in the fire of 1731 ([[William Lisle Bowles]] and [[John Gough Nichols]], ''Annals and Antiquities of Lacock Abbey: in the county of Wilts...'' London, 1835:v).</ref> Ela laid the abbey's first stone in Snail's Meadow, near the village of Lacock on 16 April 1232.<ref>Bowles and Nichols 1835:171; on the same day she founded the Carthusian priory of Henton, in Somerset, fifteen miles distant.</ref> The first of the [[Augustinian nuns]] were veiled in 1232,<ref>Date given by Bowles and Nichols 1835:81, correcting as miscopied a date MCCXXII in the lost ''Book of Lacock''.</ref> and Ela joined the community in 1238.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Garnett |first1=Oliver |title=Lacock Abbey |date=2011 |publisher=National Trust |location=Swindon |page=36}}</ref>

[[File:Lacock Abbey Chapter House, Wiltshire, UK - Diliff.jpg|thumb|left|The [[chapter house]] survives unaltered.]]
Lacock Abbey prospered throughout the [[Middle Ages]]. The rich farmlands which it had received from Ela ensured it a sizeable income from wool.<ref name="wch">{{Cite web |website=Wiltshire Community History |title=Lacock |url=https://apps.wiltshire.gov.uk/communityhistory/Community/Index/132 |publisher=Wiltshire Council |access-date=1 May 2023}}</ref>

Following the [[dissolution of the monasteries]] in the mid-16th century, [[Henry VIII]] sold the abbey to Sir [[William Sharington]] for £783. He demolished the abbey church, using the stone to extend the building, and converted the abbey into a house, starting work in about 1539. So as not to be disturbed by villagers passing close to his residence, he is said to have sold the church bells and used the proceeds to erect a bridge over the [[River Ray, Wiltshire|River Ray]] for their convenience.<ref name=BHO>{{cite book |editor-last=Pugh |editor-first=R.B. |editor2=Crittall, Elizabeth |title=A History of the County of Wiltshire, Volume 3 |publisher=British History Online |year=1956 |chapter='Houses of Augustinian canonesses: Abbey of Lacock |chapter-url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/wilts/vol3/pp303-316 }}</ref> Few other alterations were made to the monastic buildings themselves: the [[cloister]]s, for example, still stand below the living accommodation. About 1550, Sir William added an octagonal tower containing two small chambers, one above the other; the lower one was reached through the main rooms, and was for storing and viewing his treasures; the upper one, for banqueting, was only accessible by walking across the leads of the roof. In each chamber is a central octagonal stone table, carved with up-to-date Renaissance ornament.<ref>[[Mark Girouard]], ''Life in the English Country House'' 1978:106.</ref> A mid-16th century stone conduit house stands over the spring from which water was conducted to the house.<ref>Girouard 1978:248.</ref> Further additions were made over the centuries, and the house now has various grand reception rooms.<ref name="wch" />
[[File:Lacock Abbey Courtyard, Wiltshire, UK - Diliff.jpg|thumb|The internal courtyard of the cloisters]]
In the 16th and early 17th centuries, Nicholas Cooper has pointed out, bedchambers were often named for individuals who customarily inhabited them when staying at a house. At Lacock, as elsewhere, they were named for individuals "whose recognition in this way advertised the family's affinities": the best chamber was "the duke's chamber", probably signifying [[John Dudley, 1st Duke of Northumberland]], whom Sharington had served, while "Lady Thynne's chamber", identified it with the wife of Sir [[John Thynne]] of [[Longleat]], and "Mr Mildmay's chamber" was reserved for Sharington's son-in-law [[Anthony Mildmay]] of [[Apethorpe]] in Northamptonshire.<ref>Nicholas Cooper, ''Houses of the Gentry 1480–1680'' 1999:265.</ref>

[[Anne of Denmark]] came to Lacock in May 1613 during her [[Anne of Denmark and the spa at Bath|progress to Bath]]. She was in pain from gout, and her physician [[Théodore de Mayerne]] examined her and made prescriptions.<ref>[[Joseph Browne (physician)|Joseph Browne]], [https://archive.org/details/b30459709/page/10/mode/2up ''Theo. Turquet Mayernii Opera medica: Formulae Annae & Mariae'' (London, 1703), pp. 10-11]: Susannah Lyon-Whaley, [https://journals.openedition.org/hms/7196 'Hot Waters, Cold Waters, and Green Spaces: Stuart Queens Consort and Medical Treatment at English Spas', ''Histoire, Médecine et Santé'', 24 (Winter 2023), pp. 41–47] {{doi|10.4000/hms.7196}}</ref> During the [[English Civil War]] the house was garrisoned by [[Cavalier|Royalists]]. It was fortified by surrounding it with earthworks.{{sfn|Wroughton|2011}} The garrison surrendered (on agreed terms) to [[Roundhead|Parliamentarian forces]] under the command of Colonel Devereux, Governor of [[Malmesbury]], within days of Oliver Cromwell's capture of the nearby town of [[Devizes]] in late September 1645.{{sfn|Bowles|Nichols|1835|p=359}}

The house eventually passed to the Talbot family. It is most often associated with amateur scientist and inventor [[William Henry Fox Talbot]], who in 1835 made what may be the earliest surviving [[Photography|photographic]] camera [[Negative (photography)|negative]]: an interior view of the oriel window in the south gallery of the abbey.<ref>Anthony Feldman, Peter Ford (1989) ''Scientists & inventors'' p.128. Bloomsbury Books, 1989</ref><ref>''William H. Fox Talbot, inventor of the negative-positive process'' p.95. Macmillan, 1973</ref> Talbot's experiments eventually led to his invention of the more sensitive and practical [[calotype]] or "Talbotype" paper negative process for camera use, commercially introduced in 1841.<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/history/historic_figures/fox_talbot_william_henry.shtml BBC – History – Historic Figures: William Henry Fox Talbot (1800–1877)] ''[[BBC]]''</ref>

==Architecture==
[[File:Latticed window at lacock abbey 1835.jpg|thumb|upright|A latticed window in Lacock Abbey, photographed by [[William Fox Talbot]] in 1835. Shown here in positive form, this may be the oldest extant photographic negative made in a camera.]]
When Sir William Sharington purchased the remains of the Augustinian nunnery in 1540, after the dissolution, he built a country house on the cloister court. He retained the [[cloister]]s and the [[Middle Ages|medieval]] basement largely unaltered and built another storey above, so that the main rooms are on the first floor. The house is constructed of [[ashlar]] and rubble stone, the roofs are of stone slates and there are many twisted, sixteenth century chimney stacks.<ref name=BLB>{{cite web |url=http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-315553-lacock-abbey-with-stable-yard-lacock-#.V7s1kTXGD6g |title=Lacock Abbey |publisher=British Listed Buildings |access-date=22 August 2016}}</ref> The house is a blend of different styles but lacks a cohesive plan; the four wings of the house are built above the cloister passages, but the house cannot be entered from the cloisters, and the cloisters cannot be seen from inside the house.<ref>{{cite book|author=Ronnes, Hanneke |title=Architecture and Elite Culture in the United Provinces, England and Ireland, 1500-1700 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xn24enePQeoC&pg=PA79 |year=2006 |publisher=Amsterdam University Press |isbn=978-90-8555-361-8 |pages=79–80}}</ref> The abbey underwent substantial alterations in the [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] style in the 1750s, under the ownership of [[John Ivory Talbot]]. The [[great hall]] was redesigned during this period by [[Sanderson Miller]].<ref>{{ODNBweb|id=37767|title=Miller, Sanderson|first=Peter|last=Leach}}</ref>

The basement consists of an arcade of cloisters on three sides, surrounding several vaulted rooms including the [[sacristy]], [[chapter house]], and [[Calefactory|warming house]]. These rooms were situated under the original [[dormitory]]. At the other end of the building, below what was formerly the [[abbess]]' chambers and the great hall, are two rooms and the main passage. On the north side, underneath the original [[refectory]], is the [[undercroft]].<ref name=BLB/>

The west front has two flights of broad, [[Baluster|balustraded]] steps leading up to the central door. Inside is a full-height hall with a part-hipped valley roof. On either side of this are octagonal turrets with [[cupola]]s and delicately pierced [[parapet]]s. To the left of the hall is the former medieval kitchen with a balustraded parapet and [[buttress]]es. To the right is a range of parapetted rooms with a stepped buttress at the corner. The south front was plain, being the inside north wall of the original abbey church which was pulled down, but was rebuilt by William Talbot in 1828 to include bay windows. At this end of the building is Sharington's tower, an octagonal, three-storey tower, topped with a [[Belvedere (structure)|belvedere]], balustrade, and stair turret.<ref name=BLB/>

[[File:Lacock Abbey east front.jpg|thumb|The east front of Lacock Abbey]]
The east front looks more medieval than the other sides but probably dates from about 1900, however the south end cross-wing appears to be mostly sixteenth century. To the north of the house stands the well-preserved sixteenth century stable courtyard. This has timbered gabled [[dormer]] windows and a tall clock-tower at the west side of its north range. These buildings have [[mullion]] windows, and [[Tudor period|Tudor]] arched-doorways.<ref name=BLB/> Also beside the courtyard are the brewhouse, dating from the 16th century and one of the oldest in Britain,<ref>The Descent of Beer, [https://tdo-beer.com/index.php/lacock-abbey-brewhouse-brought-to-life/ Lacock Abbey Brewhouse], accessed on 8 December 2025</ref> and the bakehouse.<ref name=NatTrust>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lacock-abbey-fox-talbot-museum-and-village/features/discover-800-years-of-history-at-lacock-abbey |publisher=National Trust|title=800 years of history at Lacock Abbey |access-date=23 August 2016}}</ref> The two lodges are seventeenth century and the carriage-houses are eighteenth century.<ref name=BLB/>

==Today==
Lacock Abbey is the property of the [[National Trust]], to which it was given in 1944 by Matilda Gilchrist-Clark, who had inherited the estate from her uncle Charles Henry Fox Talbot in 1916.<ref>{{Who's Who|type=was|id=U243545|title=Talbot, Matilda Theresa}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://foxtalbot.co.uk/history-of-lacock-village-and-lacock-abbey/ |title=History of Lacock Abbey, Estate and Lacock Village |work=Fox Talbot Museum |publisher=The National Trust |access-date=23 August 2016|date=2013-08-15 }}</ref> The house, together with the stable yard, is [[Grade I listed]].<ref>{{NHLE|grade=I|desc=Lacock Abbey with stable yard|num=1283853|date=20 December 1960}}</ref>

The Fox Talbot Museum forms part of the ground floor. It celebrates the life of William Henry Fox Talbot, and his contributions to photography, and includes exhibits on the man himself,<ref name=FTM/> his mousetrap camera (so-called by his wife because he scattered the little wooden boxes round the house),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.dpreview.com/articles/7727265089 |title=Fox Talbot's historical Mousetrap camera leaves UK for first time, heads to Tokyo |author=Demolder, Damien |date=16 September 2016 |publisher=DPreview |access-date=5 September 2016}}</ref> the chemical processes involved in obtaining images and the early history of photography. Exhibitions showing the works of various photographers are sometimes held in a gallery on the first floor.<ref name=FTM>{{cite web |url=http://foxtalbot.co.uk/ |title=Fox Talbot Museum  |publisher=The National Trust |access-date=23 August 2016}}</ref> The Fenton Collection, an historic photographic collection, was transferred to the museum from the [[British Film Institute]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lacock-abbey-fox-talbot-museum-and-village/features/coming-soon-the-fenton-collection-at-lacock|title=The Fenton Collection|website=National Trust|language=en|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref>

==In film and television==
[[File:Lacock Abbey Cloisters, Wiltshire, UK - Diliff.jpg|left|upright|thumb|The cloisters of Lacock Abbey]]
Some interior sequences in ''[[Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (film)|Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone]]'' (2001) and ''[[Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (film)|Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets]]'' (2002) were filmed at Lacock, including the cloister walk where [[Harry Potter (character)|Harry]] discovers the Mirror of Erised and when he comes out from Professor Lockhart's room after serving detention and hears the [[basilisk]]. Scenes from ''[[Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (film)|Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince]]'' (2009) and ''[[Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald]]'' (2018) were also shot here.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://hpsupporters.com/hp-attractions/filming-locations/elsewhere.html |title=Harry Potter Filming Locations: Outside of London and Scotland |publisher=HP Supporters |access-date=22 August 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title='Fantastic Beasts' 2 new Lacock Abbey on-set photos show extras in Hogwarts robes – SnitchSeeker.com|url=http://www.snitchseeker.com/harry-potter-news/fantastic-beasts-2-new-lacock-abbey-on-set-photos-show-extras-in-hogwarts-robes-108348/|access-date=2021-07-05|website=snitchseeker.com}}</ref>

1121160.title: Great Chalfield Manor
1121160.extract: Great Chalfield Manor is an English country house at Great Chalfield, about 2.5 miles (4 km) northeast of the town of Bradford on Avon in the west of the county of Wiltshire.

main.*:
{{Short description|Grade I listed English country house in Wiltshire in the United Kingdom}}
{{Use British English|date=July 2021}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2021}}
[[File:Great Chalfield Manor north elevation - geograph.org.uk - 2512310.jpg|thumb|Great Chalfield: the externally symmetrical entrance front]]
'''Great Chalfield Manor''' is an [[English country house]] at [[Great Chalfield]], about {{Convert|2.5|mi|km|0}} northeast of the town of [[Bradford on Avon]] in the west of the county of [[Wiltshire]].

== History ==
[[Nikolaus Pevsner]] describes Great Chalfield as "one of the most perfect examples of the late medieval English manor house".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pevsner |first1=Nikolaus |authorlink1=Nikolaus Pevsner |last2=Cherry |first2=Bridget (revision) |year=1975 |orig-date=1963 |title=Wiltshire |series=[[Pevsner Architectural Guides#Buildings of England|The Buildings of England]] |edition=2nd |place=Harmondsworth |publisher=[[Penguin Books]] |isbn=978-0-14-0710-26-7 |pages=257–259}}</ref>

The moated [[manor house]] was built around 1465–1480 for [[Thomas Tropenell]], a modest member of the [[landed gentry]] who made a fortune as a [[cloth merchant|clothier]]. It is on the site of an earlier fortified house, of which traces remain: the bases of [[Curtain wall (architecture)|curtain walls]] to the east and north, and parts of two towers.<ref name="vch" />

The independent hall, lit on both sides, is flanked by unusually symmetrical gabled cross wings, with [[oriel window|oriel]] windows and lower gabled porches in the inner corners, in the north-facing former entrance court, for which the richest effects were reserved. Its external symmetry, unusual for its date, is superficial.<ref>Nicholas Cooper, ''Houses of the Gentry 480-1680'' 1999:60, floorplan fig.39, 61, 64.</ref> The intimately connected parish church, largely rebuilt by Tropenell, also faces into the court, which was formerly entered obliquely through a [[gatehouse]] in the west wing; Nicholas Cooper observes of the church that "the probable need to pass through the house's forecourt in order to reach it neatly demonstrates the community of secular and religious authority".<ref>Cooper 1999:64.</ref> Part of a [[moat]] survives, but the forecourt has been opened up to the outside in a manner that changes its original inward-facing aspect.<ref>A point made by Cooper 1999:61.</ref>
[[File:Great Chalfield Manor 1.jpg|thumb|left|Great Chalfield: the less formal southern aspect]]

The house passed into the Eyre family by the marriage of Ann Tropenell to [[John Eyre (died 1581)|John Eyre]] of Wedhampton in 1550. It passed down in the Eyre family for three generations until 1631 when Sir [[John Eyre (died 1639)|John Eyre]] sold it to [[Sir Richard Gurney, 1st Baronet]], [[Lord Mayor of London]]. It afterwards passed via Thomas and William Hanham, John Hall of Bradford and [[Evelyn Pierrepont, 2nd Duke of Kingston-upon-Hull]] to Robert Neale.{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

The house was altered substantially (with some of the original character lost) after the Neale family commissioned the architect [[Thomas Larkins Walker]], a pupil of [[Augustus Pugin]], to carry out a detailed survey of the manor in 1836; though his restoration proposals of 1837 were never carried out, the house was reduced and in particular, the [[great hall]], adapted as a farmhouse, lost its ornate ceiling, with only one of the original bosses surviving.{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

[[File:Great Chalfield Manor 3.jpg|thumb|One of four clipped yew garden features]]
Externally there is a garden with four "tree houses", groups of four clipped [[Taxus baccata|yew]]s that have grown together and been hollowed out inside to allow one to walk through.{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

== 20th century and today ==
The house and garden were purchased by [[George Fuller (British politician)|George Fuller]] (of [[Neston Park]]) in the early 1900s, and restored and furnished between 1905 and 1911 by his fourth son, Major Robert Fuller, under the guidance of Sir [[Harold Brakspear]].  The restoration included a sympathetic garden design by [[Alfred Parsons (artist)|Alfred Parsons]].{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

Robert Fuller gave the house and nine acres of land to the [[National Trust]] in 1943, and it is open to the public.<ref name="house">{{Cite web|url=http://www.greatchalfield.co.uk/a02.htm|title=Manor House|publisher=Robert & Patsy Fuller|access-date=30 July 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111008062334/http://www.greatchalfield.co.uk/a02.htm|archive-date=8 October 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Robert Floyd, grandson of Robert Fuller, and his family live here and manage the property for the Trust. Tours of the house are at fixed times and visitors are escorted by a guide.

[[File:Barn Doors at Great Chalfield Manor - geograph.org.uk - 310057.jpg|thumb|Doors of the barn]]
The house is [[Listed building|Grade I listed]];<ref>{{National Heritage List for England entry|num=1250902|desc=Great Chalfield Manor|access-date=5 September 2015}}</ref> the ''[[Tropenell Cartulary]]'' manuscript, compiled for Thomas Tropenell, is still kept there. The barn northwest of the house, built in the 17th and 18th centuries, is also Grade I listed,<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1263048|desc=Barn at Great Chalfield Manor|fewer-links=yes|access-date=20 April 2017}}</ref> while the gardens are Grade II listed.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England entry|num=1001232|desc=Gardens, Great Chalfield Manor|access-date=5 September 2015|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

== Church ==
[[File:Great Chalfield Manor and Church - geograph.org.uk - 310049.jpg|thumb|All Saints' Church stands close to the house]]
All Saints' Church, near the front of the house, is a small church dating from the 14th century.  It is Great Chalfield's [[Church of England parish church|parish church]], although the [[Civil parishes in England|civil parish]] was amalgamated into the newly created parish of [[Atworth]] in 1884.<ref name="vch">{{cite web|website=British History Online|title=Victoria County History: Wiltshire: Vol 7 pp59-66 - Parishes: Great Chalfield |editor-first1=R.B.|editor-last1=Pugh|editor-first2=Elizabeth|editor-last2=Crittall| author-first1=H.G.|author-last1=Chettle| author-first2=W.R.|author-last2=Powell| author-first3=P.A.|author-last3=Spalding| author-first4=P.M.|author-last4=Tillott| url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/wilts/vol7/pp59-66|publisher=University of London|date=1953|access-date=20 April 2017}}</ref>

A chapel at Great Chalfield was first mentioned in 1316; in 1428 it was a church with fewer than ten parishioners.<ref name="vch" /> The present church was built c. 1480 by Thomas Tropenell and the surviving features from that time include the south chapel, the small square [[bell-cot|bellcote]] and the roof of the nave. Robert Neale carried out improvements in 1775 which included the addition of a family chapel, now used as a vestry, to the east of the south chapel. Several windows are from the 19th century and further restoration was undertaken in 1914. The font is 13th century and the pulpit 17th.<ref name="chlisting">{{National Heritage List for England|num=1250904|desc=Church of All Saints|access-date=20 April 2017|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

Church registers survive from 1605.<ref>{{cite web|website=Wiltshire Community History|title=All Saints Parish Church, Great Chalfield|url=https://apps.wiltshire.gov.uk/communityhistory/Church/Details/10|publisher=Wiltshire Council|access-date=20 April 2017}}</ref> The building was designated as Grade I listed in 1962.<ref name="chlisting" /> Today the church is part of the benefice of Broughton Gifford, Great Chalfield & Holt.<ref>{{Cite web|date=|title=Faith in Our Village|url=https://faithinourvillage.org/|access-date=2021-07-06|language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Film location ==
The house and grounds have been used for [[location filming]] including: ''[[Wives and Daughters (1999 TV series)|Wives and Daughters]]'' (1999);<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/wiltshire/entertainment/films_and_tv/location.shtml|title=Wiltshire on film|publisher=[[BBC Online]]|access-date=26 Jan 2015|quote=Wives and Daughters: [[Dyrham Park]], NR Chippenham and Great Chalfield Manor.}}</ref> ''[[Persuasion (2007 film)|Persuasion]]'' (2007);{{Citation needed|date=July 2023}} [[The Other Boleyn Girl (2008 film)|The Other Boleyn Girl]] (2008);<ref>{{cite web|title=Houses packed with history star in Wolf Hall|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1355870235583/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=8 September 2015}}</ref> ''[[Tess of the d'Urbervilles]]'' (2008);<ref>{{cite web|title=Tess of the D'Urbervilles - Locations|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/masterpiece/tess/locations.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090118015326/http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/masterpiece/tess/locations.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=18 January 2009|publisher=PBS|access-date=8 September 2015}}</ref> [[Wolf Hall (TV series)|''Wolf Hall'']] (2014);<ref name=bbc>{{cite news|last1=Frith-Salem|first1=Benjamin|title=Wolf Halls: take a look inside the properties where the new BBC series is filmed|url=http://www.historyextra.com/feature/tudors/wolf-halls-take-look-inside-properties-where-new-bbc-series-filmed|access-date=25 January 2015|publisher=BBC History Magazine|date=20 January 2015}}</ref> ''[[Poldark (2015 TV series)|Poldark]]'' (2015);<ref>{{Cite web|title=Poldark: behind the scenes|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/cornish-coast-stars-in-poldark-remake|access-date=2021-07-04|website=National Trust|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Poldark: Our guide to the upcountry locations from Frome to Berkeley Castle|url=https://www.radiotimes.com/travel/poldark-our-guide-to-the-upcountry-locations-from-frome-to-berkeley-castle/|access-date=2021-07-04|website=Radio Times|language=en}}</ref> and [[The White Princess (miniseries)|''The White Princess'']] (2017).{{Citation needed|date=July 2023}} For ''[[Wolf Hall: The Mirror and the Light]]'' (2024), scenes were shot in the study and in the Great Hall, while exterior filming was done in the Arts and Crafts gardens.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/masterpiece/specialfeatures/wolf-hall-the-mirror-and-the-light-filming-locations/#:~:text=Great%20Chalfield%20Manor%20and%20Garden,in%20Wolf%20Hall%20Season%201|title=Wolf Hall: The Mirror and the Light Filming Locations|date=30 March 2025|work=Masterpiece Newsletter  |access-date=5 May 2025 |quote=We picked the site because of its atmosphere and because the rooms lead nicely onto each other}}</ref>

2666928.title: Stonehenge Landscape
2666928.extract:
The Stonehenge Landscape is a property of The National Trust, located on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England. The estate (formerly known as Stonehenge Historic Landscape and before that as Stonehenge Down) covers 2,100 acres (850 ha) surrounding the Neolithic monument of Stonehenge, which is administered by English Heritage.  Much of the land is designated open access by the Trust, including the fields immediately around Stonehenge and other fields that become available as part of the chalk grassland reversion project (see below). Stonehenge itself is in the care of English Heritage, having been given to the nation in 1918 by Cecil and Mary Chubb, who had bought it three years previously from the Antrobus family.
Much of the land surrounding the stones was acquired in 1927 after a public appeal was launched to prevent further development on the fields around the monument. The successfully purchased land was given to the National Trust for the benefit of the nation.  Shortly afterwards such structures as cottages and the World War I-era Stonehenge Aerodrome were removed from the immediate vicinity of the stones. 
There are two memorials to different fatal flying accidents in the area. Eustace Loraine and Staff Sergeant Wilson were killed in 1912 near the new Stonehenge Visitors' centre. Major Hewetson was killed in a flying accident near Fargo Wood in July 1913. Later the Trust acquired more land, principally after the purchase of an adjacent farm in the early 21st century.
The land owned by the Trust comprises almost one third of the Stonehenge World Heritage Site, and contains nearly 400 ancient monuments (most of them scheduled).  These monuments include the enormous earthwork known as the Stonehenge Cursus, the Avenue, Woodhenge and Durrington Walls, as well as numerous burial mounds known as barrows.  The estate also includes some of the Nile Clumps, large clumps of trees on arable farmland, said to represent ship positions at the Battle of the Nile. This is said to form a large memorial to Horatio Nelson, created by a local landowner after Nelson's death. 
During the 1970s and 1980s, the estate was the scene of the Stonehenge Free Festival.  Damage to monuments such as the Cursus barrows was one of the reasons that the festival was banned in 1985.
As part of the World Heritage Site Management Plan for Stonehenge, some 340 hectares of the land will revert to chalk grassland by 2011.  The scheme (one of the largest reversion schemes of its kind in Europe) will turn over much of the estate to permanent pasture, and allow for increased open access around the area.  At present some 112 hectares have reverted and, along with the existing grassland, are used as public open access as well as animal grazing.

4580394.extract: Dinton is a village, civil parish and former manor in Wiltshire, England, in the Nadder valley on the B3089 road about 8 miles (13 km) west of Salisbury. The parish population was 696 at the 2011 census, estimated at 733 in 2019. The civil parish includes the village of Baverstock, about 1 mile (1.6 km) east of Dinton village.

'''Dinton''' is a village, [[Civil parishes in England|civil parish]] and former [[Lord of the manor|manor]] in Wiltshire, England, in the [[River Nadder|Nadder]] valley on the [[B3089 road]] about {{convert|8|mi|km|0}} west of [[Salisbury]]. The parish population was 696 at the 2011 census,<ref name=Census/> estimated at 733 in 2019.<ref>[https://citypopulation.de/en/uk/southwestengland/admin/wiltshire/E04011697__dinton/ City Population. Retrieved 11 March 2021.]</ref> The civil parish includes the village of [[Baverstock]], about {{convert|1|mi}} east of Dinton village.

==History==
The northern bounds of the parish follow a prehistoric line known as [[Grim's Ditch]], through downland overlooking the [[River Wylye|Wylye]] valley further north.<ref name="vch"/><ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1005606 |desc=Grim's Ditch |access-date=17 June 2016}}</ref> Hanging Langford Camp, an [[Iron Age]] settlement, is just beyond the parish boundary.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1005602 |desc=Hanging Langford camp and Church-end Ring |access-date=17 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref> The [[hillfort]] known as Wick Ball Camp lies near the western boundary of the parish, partly within Dinton Park.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1005673 |desc=Wick Ball Camp, The Common |access-date=17 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

A [[Roman roads in Britain|Roman road]] from the Mendip lead mines to Old Sarum passed east–west, just south of the ditch.<ref name="vch"/> The Domesday Book of 1086 recorded a settlement of 37 households at Dinton, held by [[Shaftesbury Abbey]].<ref>{{OpenDomesday |SU0131 |dinton |Dinton}}</ref>

After the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries|Dissolution]] in 1540, much of Dinton's land was acquired by the [[Earls of Pembroke]]. Later other land was purchased by the Wyndham family, which created Dinton Park. All Pembroke and Wyndham land was sold in the 20th century.<ref name="wch">{{Cite web |website=Wiltshire Community History |title=Dinton |url=https://apps.wiltshire.gov.uk/communityhistory/Community/Index/79 |publisher=Wiltshire Council |access-date=17 June 2016}}</ref>

Dinton had a school from an early date, with some 80 children attending in 1818.<ref name="vch"/> A [[National school (England and Wales)|National School]] was built in 1872 and took children of all ages until 1935, when those over 11 transferred to Wilton. The school became a Church of England [[voluntary controlled school]] in 1945.<ref>{{Cite web |website=Wiltshire Community History |title=Dinton Church of England VC Primary School |url=https://apps.wiltshire.gov.uk/communityhistory/School/Details/1364 |publisher=Wiltshire Council |access-date=17 June 2016}}</ref>

[[File:Dinton station (remains) geograph-3412970-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg|thumb|right|The station buildings in 1994]]
The [[Salisbury and Yeovil Railway]] was built across the parish in 1859, passing to the south of Dinton and Baverstock. [[Dinton railway station|Dinton station]] was south-west of the village on a lane towards Fovant. The station closed in 1966.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Oakley |first1=Mike |title=Wiltshire Railway Stations |date=2004 |publisher=The Dovecote Press |location=Wimborne |isbn=1904349331 |pages=56–57}}</ref> A branch called the Fovant Military Railway, {{convert|2+1/2|mi|km}} in length, ran south from near the station to the military camps around Fovant; it was opened in 1915 and closed in 1920.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fovant Military Railway |url=http://www.fovanthistory.org/railway.html |website=Fovant History Interest Group |access-date=17 June 2016}}</ref>

In 1934 the parish was extended eastwards to absorb the ancient parish of Baverstock.<ref name="vch"/> Before, during and after the Second World War, the area was used for storing military equipment and ammunition. Some of these premises were outposts of [[RAF Chilmark]].<ref>{{Cite web |website=British History Online |title=Victoria County History – Wiltshire – Vol 13 pp114-125 – Parishes: Chilmark |editor-first=D. A. |editor-last=Crowley |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/wilts/vol13/pp114-125 |publisher=University of London |access-date=17 June 2016}}</ref>

==Churches==
<!-- Church of St Mary, Dinton redirects here -->

===St Mary, Dinton===
[[File:St. Mary the Virgin Church, Dinton.jpg|thumb|St Mary's Church]]
The [[Church of England parish church]] of St Mary the Virgin, begun in the late 12th century, is a [[Listed building#Categories of listed building|Grade I listed]] building. The north doorway survives from the earliest work, while the rest of the church is largely from the 13th and 14th centuries. [[Victorian restoration|Restoration]] by [[William Butterfield]] in 1873–1875 included adding a south vestry and north porch.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1146120 |desc=Church of St Mary the Virgin |access-date=16 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref> The tower has six bells, one from the 14th century and two from the 16th.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dinton, St Mary |url=https://dove.cccbr.org.uk/detail.php?DoveID=DINTON%20WIL |website=Dove's Guide for Church Bell Ringers |access-date=16 June 2016}}</ref>

Until the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries|Dissolution]], Dinton was a [[prebend]] of [[Shaftesbury Abbey]]. St Edward's at [[Teffont Magna]] was a [[chapelry]] of Dinton until 1922.<ref name="vch">{{Cite web |website=British History Online |title=Victoria County History – Wiltshire – Vol 8, Warminster, Westbury and Whorwellsdown Hundreds, pp25-34 – Dinton |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/wilts/vol8/pp25-34 |publisher=University of London |access-date=16 June 2016}}</ref> Today the church is part of the Nadder Valley team ministry, which also covers Baverstock and Teffont.<ref>{{Cite web |title=St Mary, Dinton |url=https://www.achurchnearyou.com/dinton/ |website=A Church Near You |access-date=16 June 2016}}</ref>

===St Editha, Baverstock===
The church at [[Baverstock]], dedicated to [[Edith of Wilton]], is from the 14th–15th centuries, with restoration in 1880–1893 by Butterfield. It is Grade II* listed.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1283631 |desc=Church of St Edith of Wilton |access-date=16 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

==Notable buildings==
Three listed houses are now owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]].

Hyde's House, near Dinton church, is a Grade I listed former rectory, an early 18th-century rebuilding of an earlier house. Together with Philipps House and Dinton Park, it was given to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] by Bertram Philips in 1943.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1146122 |desc=Hydes House with attached walls and gatepiers |access-date=19 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

[[Philipps House]], formerly Dinton House, was built in 1816 by William IV Wyndham (1769–1841) to designs by Sir [[Jeffry Wyatville]], replacing a 17th-century house. The house stands in formal gardens and parkland known as Dinton Park. In 1916 the estate was bought by Bertram Philipps, who renamed the house after himself.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1318756 |desc=Phillips House |access-date=19 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref><ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1001231 |desc=Dinton Park |access-date=19 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

Little Clarendon, also Grade II* listed, is a late 17th-century former farmhouse. The house was restored in the early 20th century by George Herbert Engleheart (died 1936), a noted breeder of daffodils. His widow gave the house to the National Trust in 1940.<ref name="vch"/><ref name="wch"/><ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1146116 |desc=Little Clarendon |access-date=19 June 2016 |fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

==Present day==
The parish has local services, including two [[public house]]s and a village hall.

The railway remains open as part of the [[West of England Main Line|London Waterloo to Exeter]] line; the nearest station is {{stnlink|Tisbury}}. The village school continues on the same site as Dinton C of E Primary School.

The [[Monarch's Way]] long-distance footpath crosses the parish north of Dinton, leaving via Grovely Wood.

==Descent of the manor==
The manor estate of Dinton and Over Teffont (now [[Teffont Magna]]) belonged to Shaftesbury Abbey from before the Norman Conquest<ref name="vch"/> until the Dissolution, when it passed rapidly through the hands of various Tudor property speculators. It was granted in 1540 to [[Sir Thomas Arundell]] (died 1552), who immediately sold it, having obtained a [[licence of alienation]], to Matthew Colthurst, who sold it in turn to [[William Green (died 1555)|William Green]] of Heale, in [[Woodford, Wiltshire|Woodford]].

In 1547 the entire manor gained a long-term owner when it was granted to [[William Herbert, 1st Earl of Pembroke (10th Creation)|Sir William Herbert]] (1501–1570), later 1st [[Earl of Pembroke]]. It remained part of the family's nearby estate of [[Wilton House|Wilton]] until 1918, when it was sold in lots and dismembered.<ref name="vch"/>

==Subsidiary estates==
===Hyde===
[[File:HydeArmorials.PNG|thumb|upright|Arms of Hyde: ''Azure, a chevron between three lozenges or'']]
The [[rectory]] and [[advowson]] of Dinton were sold in 1585 by [[Henry Herbert, 2nd Earl of Pembroke]] (1534–1601) to [[Lawrence Hyde (died 1590)|Lawrence Hyde I]] (died 1590) of West Hatch, MP for Heytesbury in 1584.<ref>[http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1558-1603/member/hyde-lawrence-i-1590 History of Parliament biography of Lawrence Hyde I]</ref> His eldest son Robert Hyde I sold them in 1594 to his brother Sir [[Lawrence Hyde (attorney-general)|Lawrence Hyde II]] (1562–1641), attorney-general to [[Anne of Denmark]], wife of King James I. They were inherited by the latter's son [[Robert Hyde (judge)|Sir Robert Hyde II]] (died 1665), Chief Justice of Common Pleas, who died without surviving issue, and then passed to his nephew, Robert Hyde III (died 1722), son of [[Alexander Hyde]], Bishop of Salisbury. Robert III died without progeny and bequeathed the rectory and advowson to his cousin Rev. Robert Hyde IV (died 1723), a Fellow of [[Magdalen College, Oxford]], who in turn passed them to his college, which retained them until 1950, when they passed to the Bishop of Salisbury.<ref name="vch"/>
 
The brother of Sir Lawrence Hyde II, lay rector of Dinton, was [[Henry Hyde (died 1634)|Henry Hyde]] (c. 1563–1634), MP, father of the statesman [[Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon]] (1609–1674), who was born at Dinton.<ref name=Holmes>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11410 ''Wanderings in Wessex'' by Edric Holmes.], Chapter X. Available as a [[Project Gutenberg]] ebook.</ref> The estate of ''Little Clarendon'' is within the parish of Dinton, and was apparently the origin of the appellation he chose for his earldom. Henry Hyde appears to have leased the rectory and advowson of Dinton from his brother, and it was probably in the rectory house that the future Earl of Clarendon was born.  Henry Hyde moved away to Purton between 1623 and 1625.<ref name="vch"/>

===Wyndham===
[[File:WyndhamArms.jpg|thumb|upright|Arms of Wyndham: ''Azure, a chevron between three lion's heads erased or'']] 
The descent of another estate in Dinton in the Wyndham family went as follows:<ref name="Burke's Landed Gentry 1937">Burke's Landed Gentry, 1937, p. 2511, pedigree of Wyndham.</ref>
*William I Wyndham (1659–1734) bought the manor in 1689.<ref name="vch"/> He was the third son of [[Wadham Wyndham (judge)|Sir Wadham Wyndham]] (1609–1668), of [[Norrington Manor|Norrington]], Wiltshire, a judge of the [[Court of King's Bench (England)|King's Bench]] and ninth son of [[John Wyndham (1558–1645)|Sir John Wyndham]] (1558–1645) of [[Orchard Wyndham]], Somerset.<ref name="Burke's Landed Gentry 1937"/> William I married Henrietta Stratford, a daughter and co-heiress of Henry Stratford of [[Hawling]], Gloucestershire.
*William II Windham (died 1762), eldest son, inherited Dinton from his father and Hawling from his mother. He married Barbara Smith, daughter and heiress of Michael Smith of [[Stanton St Bernard]], Wiltshire.
*William III Wyndham (died 1786), eldest son, of Dinton and Hawling, was a pioneer in agricultural improvement.<ref name="vch"/> He married in 1767 Elizabeth Heathcote (died 1809), a daughter of [[Heathcote baronets|Sir Thomas Heathcote, 2nd Baronet]] (1721–1787), of [[Hursley House|Hursley Park]], Southampton.
*William IV Wyndham (1769–1841), eldest son, of Dinton, inherited the manor of [[Norrington Manor|Norrington]] from his Wyndham cousin, descended from the eldest son of the judge Sir Wadham Wyndham (died 1668). He married in 1794 Laetitia Popham (died 1837), daughter of Alexander Popham, a [[Master in Chancery]]. In 1816 he built the present house to designs by Sir [[Jeffry Wyattville]]. 
*[[William Wyndham (1796–1862)|William V Wyndham]] (1796–1862), of Dinton, eldest son, [[Justice of the Peace|JP]], [[Deputy Lieutenant|DL]], [[Member of Parliament|MP]] for [[Wiltshire South (UK Parliament constituency)|Wiltshire South]] 1852–1859, married in 1831 Ellen Heathcote (died 1883), eldest daughter of Rev. Samuel Heathcote of Bramshaw Hill, Hampshire.
*William VI Wyndham (1834–1914), eldest son, JP, DL, of Dinton, was [[heir male]] to his grandfather under the will of a distant cousin [[George Wyndham, 4th Earl of Egremont|George Francis Wyndham]] (1786–1845), who shared descent from Sir John Wyndham (1558–1645) of Orchard Wyndham, after the death in 1876 of the 4th Earl's widow, who had retained a life interest.<ref name="Burke's LG">Burke's LG.</ref> He thus inherited the ancient family manor of Orchard Wyndham. He married in 1867 Frances Ann Stafford (died 1934), second daughter of Rev. Charles James Stafford, vicar of Dinton.
*William VII Wyndham (born 1868), eldest son, JP, of Orchard Wyndham, sold Dinton in 1916 to Bertram Philipps.<ref name="Burke's LG"/>

'''Mompesson House''' is an 18th-century house in the Cathedral Close, [[Salisbury]], [[Wiltshire]], England. The house is [[Grade I listed]]<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|desc=Mompesson House|num= 1355808 |accessdate=16 December 2019}}</ref> and has been in the ownership of the [[National Trust]] since 1975.<ref name="sccps">{{cite web | last = | first = | author-link = | title = Mompesson House | website = | publisher = Salisbury Cathedral Close Preservation Society | date = | url = http://salisburyclosepreservation.org/momp2.htm#Top%20of%20Page | format = | doi = | accessdate = 18 May 2013 }}</ref>

==History==
The Mompesson family had lived in Wiltshire since the fifteenth century, residing in [[Bathampton]].{{sfn|Reiff|1986|p=110}} Thomas Mompesson the elder moved to Salisbury, securing a 40-year lease on the north side of Chorister's Green in 1635 and building a large property with a hall and ten other rooms.{{sfn|Reiff|1986|p=110}} His son, Sir [[Thomas Mompesson]], [[Member of parliament|MP]] for the [[Salisbury (UK Parliament constituency)|constituency of Salisbury]] in 1679, 1695 and 1701, rebuilt the property in the late 1670s as well as adding the adjacent stable block.{{sfn|Reiff|1986|p=111}} The site was purchased at the end of the 17th century and the house reflects the classic [[Queen Anne style architecture|Queen Anne style]] of that period, as well as the influence of [[Christopher Wren]].{{sfn|Stratton|1920|p=25}} It is built with ashlar [[Chilmark stone]].<ref name=NHLE/><ref name="bbc">{{cite web | last = | first = | author-link = | title = Your Paintings | website =[[Art UK]]| date = | url = https://artuk.org/visit/venues/national-trust-mompesson-house-4987  | format = | doi = | accessdate = 18 May 2013  }}</ref> To the right of the main house stands the brick-built service building which was constructed on the site of the old Eagle Inn that closed in 1625. 

Thomas's son Charles completed the building in 1701; his initials{{sfn|Reiff|1986|p=111}} and date can be seen on the heads of the water downpipes.{{sfn|Pevsner|Cherry|2002|p=429}}  The renovations included a new stone façade, and created the building seen today.{{sfn|Reiff|1986|p=111}} In 1703 Charles commemorated his marriage to Elizabeth Longueville by adding a cartouche over the front door displaying their joined coats of arms.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=4}} After Charles' death in 1714, Elizabeth's brother [[Charles Longueville]] moved into the house with his widowed sister. They added the plasterwork, staircase and the brick wing in 1740.{{sfn|Reiff|1986|p=113}} After Charles Longueville's death, he attempted to leave the house to his natural-born son, John Clark. However, Elizabeth refused to administer his will and instead added a codicil to her own will stipulating that John Clark would only have the right to use the house for his lifetime, after which the house would pass to Mr Thomas Hayter of Salisbury.<ref>The National Archives; Kew, Surrey, England; Records of the Prerogative Court of Canterbury, Series PROB 11; Class: PROB 11; Piece: 790</ref>

Next, the house was occupied by Ann Wyndham, the widowed Mrs [[Henry Portman]] and her three daughters, Ann Mary, Henrietta, and Wyndham. {{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=22}} Henrietta was the last of the sisters to die in 1846 and her son transferred the lease to William Oliver Colt, the brother-in-law of George Barnard Townsend. The Townsend family occupied the house from 1846 to 1939, and the flamboyant artist Miss Barbara Townsend, mentioned in [[Edith Olivier]]'s book ''Four Victorian Ladies of Wiltshire'', lived there for almost all of her 96 years.<ref>{{cite web | last = | first = | author-link = | title = Salisbury Journal | work = Wonderful Water colours | publisher = Newsquest Southern (Ltd) | date = 23 June 2011| url = http://www.salisburyjournal.co.uk/leisure/entertainments/9102019.Wonderful_watercolours/ | format = | doi = | accessdate = 18 May 2013 }}</ref> In 1946, the Dean and Chapter of Salisbury Cathedral negotiated with the Church Commissioners to transfer ownership of the Bishop's Palace to accommodate the ever-expanding Cathedral School. In return, the Church Commissioners received Mompesson House as the new Bishop's residence, occupied by Geoffrey Lunt and William Anderson, though the latter found the house too small and moved out in 1951.

In 1952 the freehold was purchased from the [[Church Commissioners]] by the architect, Denis Martineau, who immediately bequeathed it to the National Trust, though continued to live in the house until his death in 1975.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=24}} Martineau completed extensive repairs and renovation throughout the property and opened the home to visitors two afternoons each week.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=24}} The National Trust spent the next two years redecorating the property and acquiring a suitable collection of furniture, before the house opened to the public in May 1977.

The [[overthrow (structure)|overthrow]], iron railings, gates and iron lamps at the front of the building are Grade I listed separately from the house.<ref name=NHLE2>{{NHLE|desc=Screen wall, rails, piers, gates and overthrow in front of Mompesson House|num= 1253989 |accessdate=16 December 2019}}</ref>

== Collections ==
[[File:The Dining Room at Mompesson House.jpg|thumb|left|upright|The dining room at Mompesson House]]
The house contains Georgian plasterwork and carvings of exceptional quality which have been carefully restored by the National Trust, including the removal of many layers of paint which had obscured them.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=24}} When the Trust inherited the house, it was empty of furnishings as Martineau had bequeathed his possessions to relatives.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=24}} The Trust has therefore redecorated the visitor rooms with 18th-century pieces.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=24}}

In keeping with the Georgian interiors, the dining room in the house is used to display the Turnbull collection of English 18th-century drinking glasses bequeathed to the Trust in 1970 by Mr. O.G.N. Turnbull.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Newby |first1=Martine S |title=The Turnbull collection of English 18th-Century drinking glasses |publisher=National Trust | date=2006 |location=Swindon |isbn=1-903394-02-3}}</ref> The house also hosts the Bessemer-Wright collection of ceramics, bequeathed by Mrs Adam Smith,{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=24}} which includes porcelain figures from the [[Derby Porcelain|Derby]] & [[Bow porcelain factory|Bow]] factories, [[Manufacture nationale de Sèvres|Sèvres]] plates and [[Wedgwood|Wedgewood]] urns.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=6}}

==In popular culture==
Mompesson House was used as a location for the 1995 film adaptation of ''[[Sense and Sensibility (1995 film)|Sense and Sensibility]]''.{{sfn|Garnett|2008|p=24}}

19685578.title: Philipps House
19685578.extract:
Philipps House (until 1916 Dinton House) is an early 19th-century Neo-Grecian country house at Dinton, overlooking the Nadder valley about 8 miles (13 km) west of Salisbury, Wiltshire, England. The house was built in 1816 by William Wyndham to the designs of Sir Jeffry Wyatville, replacing a 17th-century house. In 1916 the estate was bought by Bertram Philipps, who renamed the house after himself, then in 1943 gave the house and grounds to the National Trust. The is Grade II* listed and its parkland (known as Dinton Park is Grade II* on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens.
The house is built of Chilmark stone, a local stone also used for Salisbury Cathedral, and Wyatt is believed to have based his design on Pythouse, some seven miles (11 km) away at Newtown, near Tisbury. The house is two-storied with symmetrically set chimney stacks and a central lantern. The main (south) front has nine bays with an Ionic portico. The rooms are planned around a spacious square hall with an imperial staircase to the first floor. The house is one of the first in England to have a central heating system installed, which was achieved by pumping hot air from a boiler in the basement into the stairwell.

main.*:
{{Short description|Country house in Dinton, Wiltshire, England}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
{{Use British English|date=February 2023}}
[[File:Philipps House view from southwest on sunny summer day.jpg|thumb|Philipps House]]
[[File:Philipps House 1.jpg|thumb|Philipps House]]

'''Philipps House''' (until 1916 '''Dinton House'''<ref>Burke's Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Landed Gentry, 15th Edition, ed. Pirie-Gordon, H., London, 1937, p.2512, Dinton House sold by Wyndham family in 1916</ref>) is an early 19th-century Neo-Grecian [[English country house|country house]] at [[Dinton, Wiltshire|Dinton]], overlooking the [[River Nadder|Nadder]] valley about {{convert|8|mi|km|0|abbr=}} west of [[Salisbury]], Wiltshire, England. The house was built in 1816 by William Wyndham to the designs of Sir [[Jeffry Wyatville]], replacing a 17th-century house. In 1916 the estate was bought by Bertram Philipps, who renamed the house after himself, then in 1943 gave the house and grounds to the [[National Trust]]. The is [[Listed building#Categories of listed building|Grade II* listed]]<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1318756|desc=Phillips House|access-date=20 June 2016}}</ref> and its parkland (known as Dinton Park is Grade II* on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1001231|desc=Dinton Park|access-date=20 June 2016|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

The house is built of [[Chilmark Quarries|Chilmark stone]], a local stone also used for [[Salisbury Cathedral]], and Wyatt is believed to have based his design on [[Pythouse]], some {{convert|7|mi|km|spell=in}} away at Newtown, near [[Tisbury, Wiltshire|Tisbury]]. The house is two-storied with symmetrically set chimney stacks and a central lantern. The main (south) front has nine bays with an [[Ionic order|Ionic]] portico. The rooms are planned around a spacious square hall with an [[imperial staircase]] to the first floor. The house is one of the first in England to have a central heating system installed, which was achieved by pumping hot air from a boiler in the basement into the stairwell.<ref name="vch">{{cite web|website=British History Online|title=Victoria County History: Wiltshire: Vol 8 pp25-34: Dinton|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/wilts/vol8/pp25-34|publisher=University of London|access-date=20 June 2016}}</ref>

==History==
The house was designed by Jeffry Wyatt, later Sir [[Jeffry Wyatville]] for William Wyndham (1769–1841), a descendant of Sir [[Wadham Wyndham (judge)|Wadham Wyndam]],<ref name="vch" /> and was built between 1814 and 1817 on the site of an earlier, demolished seventeenth-century house, Dinton House, which had been the Wyndham family home since 1689. It was sold in 1916 by William Wyndham (1868–1951) of [[Orchard Wyndham]] in Somerset, whose father William VI Wyndham (1834–1914), of Dinton House, had inherited Orchard Wyndham as [[heir male]] to his grandfather William IV Wyndham (1769–1841), of Dinton, under the will of his distant cousin [[George Wyndham, 4th Earl of Egremont]] (1786–1845) (who shared common descent from Sir [[John Wyndham (1558-1645)]] of Orchard Wyndham).<ref>Burke's Landed Gentry, 1937, p.2511, pedigree of Wyndham</ref>

In 1917 foreclosure proceedings were brought against Dinton House and its estate. The estate was bought by Bertram Erasmus Philipps (1870–1947), a descendant of the [[Philipps baronets]] of [[Picton Castle]] (1621 creation);<ref>{{cite book|author=Arthur Charles Fox-Davies|title=Armorial Families|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KDw6AQAAMAAJ|year=1895|publisher=Jack|page=787}}</ref><ref>Bertram was the 5th son of the Reverend Sir James Erasmus Philipps, 12th baronet, of Picton Castle, Vicar of [[Warminster]], Wiltshire. His brothers were [[John Philipps, 1st Viscount St Davids]]; [[Owen Philipps, 1st Baron Kylsant]]; Major-General Sir [[Ivor Philipps]]; and [[Laurence Philipps, 1st Baron Milford]]; several of them were [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Members of Parliament]] and directors or stockholders in the [[Royal Mail Steam Packet Company]] and other shipping companies.</ref> who renamed the house after himself. He was [[High Sheriff of Wiltshire]] in 1923.<ref>[https://artuk.org/visit/venues/national-trust-philipps-house-dinton-4993 "Philipps House," ''Art UK – Your Paintings''], accessed 22 June 2013.</ref><ref>[http://www.dicamillocompanion.com/houses_detail.asp?ID=1601 "Philipps House (Dinton House)," ''The DiCamillo Companion''], accessed 22 June 2013.</ref>  Philipps and his wife, who had no children, annually hosted the pupils from the village school for a tea party at Philipps House with sports and fireworks.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dinton Church of England VC Primary School|url=https://apps.wiltshire.gov.uk/communityhistory/School/Details/1364|website=Wiltshire Community History|publisher=Wiltshire Council|access-date=20 June 2016}}</ref>

In 1936, Philipps leased the house to the [[YWCA]] and moved to nearby Hyde's House, a former rectory which he had bought in 1924 and where he lived until his death.<ref>[http://www.wiltshire-opc.org.uk/Items/Dinton%20-%20Andrews%20Newspaper%20Index%20Cards%201937-1947.pdf "Dinton – Andrews Newspaper Index Cards, 1790–1976," Wiltshire OPC, 2011, accessed 22 June 2013]</ref><ref>[http://www.southwilts.com/site/Dinton-Recreation-Ground/text-index.htm "Dinton Recreation Ground," South Wiltshire Strategic Alliance, accessed 22 June 2013]</ref><ref>Philipps died intestate on 10 February 1947 at [[Menton, France]], where he was staying with his wife, Florence, who died a week earlier on February 4. Philipps's brother Laurence Philipps, 1st Baron Milford, was subsequently appointed his personal representative for the probate of his estate.</ref> During World War II, the park in front of Philipps House was requisitioned for use by the [[United States Army Air Force]], who erected a number of [[Nissen hut]]s there. In 1943 Philipps gave the house and {{convert|250|acre|km2}} of parkland to the [[National Trust]], along with Hyde's House as well as a number of paintings owned by the Wyndham and Philipps families.<ref name="nt">{{cite web|title=Dinton Park and Philipps House|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dinton-park-and-philipps-house|website=National Trust|access-date=20 June 2016}}</ref>

== National Trust ==
Although the house and estate became the property of the National Trust, the property was handed over on the condition that it would continue to be leased to the YWCA, on a [[peppercorn rent]], for as long as they had use for it. During their occupation the house was predominantly used as an artists' retreat, providing residential art courses for amateur and semi-professional painters.{{Citation needed|date=February 2019}}

The interior spaces were converted into artist studios with bedrooms available for paying guests. The grounds and outlying area also provided locations for landscape painting.{{Citation needed|date=February 2019}}

The YWCA remained at Philipps House until 1995. Despite the art courses being as heavily subscribed to as ever, the withdrawal of the YWCA was inevitable after the terms of the lease were changed when it was presented to the YWCA for renewal, a process that occurred every ten years. The lease transferred the cost of maintaining the structure of the house and other amenities from the National Trust to the YWCA at a time when many major works were due, such as laying new pipes from the neighbouring village of Dinton.{{Citation needed|date=February 2019}}

After the YWCA left, the National Trust carried out a refurbishment of the house, which was leased to a tenant family. As of March 2023, the house remains closed to the public. The parkland that surrounds the house is still known as Dinton Park, and is accessible to the public.<ref name="nt" />

56915242.title: The Pepperbox
56915242.extract: The Pepperbox, also known as Eyre's Folly, is a folly tower that stands near the highest point on Pepperbox Hill, the peak of a chalk ridge about 5 miles (8 km) south-east of the city of Salisbury, Wiltshire, England. Built in 1606 by Giles Eyre, the folly is a three-storey hexagonal tower constructed of brick, with its entrances and windows blocked up. The building's original purpose is unknown, though theories include that it was built to provide Eyre with views of Longford Castle or to provide local landowners' wives, including Eyre's wife Jane, with a lookout tower to watch the hunt. The tower is considered one of the oldest follies, and is a Grade II listed building. The tower and hillside are owned by the National Trust.

'''The Pepperbox''', also known as '''Eyre's Folly''', is a [[folly]] tower that stands near the highest point on Pepperbox Hill, the peak of a chalk ridge about {{Convert|5|mi|km|0|abbr=}} south-east of the city of [[Salisbury]], Wiltshire, England. Built in 1606 by Giles Eyre, the folly is a three-storey hexagonal tower constructed of brick, with its entrances and windows blocked up. The building's original purpose is unknown, though theories include that it was built to provide Eyre with views of [[Longford Castle]] or to provide local landowners' wives, including Eyre's wife Jane, with a lookout tower to watch the hunt. The tower is considered one of the oldest follies, and is a [[Grade II listed building]]. The tower and hillside are owned by the [[National Trust]].

==Origins and purpose==
Although the [[Historic England]] listing dates The Pepperbox to the early 18th century,<ref name=":0">{{National Heritage List for England|num=1355631|desc=The Pepperbox|access-date=3 January 2021}}</ref> it is accepted that the tower was built in 1606 by Giles Eyre of the nearby Brickworth House, hence the alternate name "Eyre's Folly".<ref name="Headley">{{cite book|last1=Headley|first1=Gwyn|title=Follies: Fabulous, Fanciful and Frivolous Buildings|date=19 July 2012|publisher=National Trust Books|location=England|isbn=978-1907892301|page=69}}</ref> Eyre is known for being the father of settler [[John Eyre (settler)|John Eyre]] and grandfather of [[Giles Eyre]], a judge.<ref>{{cite book | last = Burke | first = Sir Bernard | editor = Arthur Charles Fox-Davies | title = A Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Landed Gentry of Ireland | url = https://archive.org/details/genealogicalhera00burkuoft | publisher=Harrison & Sons | location = London | date = 1912 }}</ref> The original purpose of the tower is unknown.<ref name="Quinn" /> One theory is that Eyre was envious of [[Longford Castle]], recently built by [[Thomas Gorges|Sir Thomas Gorges]], and built the Pepperbox to overlook the castle; the epitaph on Eyre's gravestone describes him as "a man much oppressed by publick power."<ref name="Meulenkamp" /> Another is that the tower was built as a hunting stand,<ref name="Meulenkamp" /> perhaps so the local landowners' wives – including Eyre's wife Jane, whom he married in 1603 – could watch the hunt in comfort without being exposed to public gaze.<ref name="Headley" /><ref name="Quinn" /> In their book ''Follies, Grottoes and Garden Building'', Gwen Headley and Wim Meulenkamp consider the hunting stand theory to be "saner" given that the tower lacks a "folly atmosphere".<ref name="Meulenkamp" /> One account states: "It can be counted as a folly but may have been used a lookout so that ladies could follow the progress of the hunt, away from the rain and mud".<ref name="Wiltshire">{{Cite web |date=14 March 2003 |title=Question: What is the history of the Pepperbox of Pepperbox Hill? |website=[[Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre]] |url=https://apps.wiltshire.gov.uk/communityhistory/Question/Details/100 |publisher=Wiltshire Council |access-date=26 May 2023}}</ref>

It has alternately been suggested that the 1606 date is an erroneous dating due to a coincidence of names, and that the tower was more probably built by Eyres' great-great-grandson Giles Eyre (1664–1734) in the early 18th century. The elder Giles Eyre was the first of five generations of owners with the same name covering the period from 1606 to 1750 and by the time the younger Eyres owned the Brickworth estate, it had grown to include the land on which the Pepperbox stands, which had not been the case in 1606.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.younsmere-frustfield.org.uk/Whiteparish/Brickworth.htm|title = Brickworth (Estate)}}</ref>

==Description and location==
[[File:Approach to the Pepperbox - geograph.org.uk - 1902884.jpg|thumb|Approach to the Pepperbox across the chalk downs]]

The Pepperbox is a hexagonal, three-storey tower constructed of English [[bond (brick)|bond brick]], with a low, pyramidal [[Welsh slate]] roof that was rebuilt around 1900, topped by a [[weather vane]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Whitelaw" /> The ground floor's doorways are segmental-headed,<ref name=":0" /> indicating the building originally stood on open arches.<ref name="Meulenkamp">{{cite book|last1=Headley|first1=Gwen|last2=Meulenkamp|first2=Wim|title=Follies, Grottoes and Garden Buildings|date=16 June 1999|publisher=Aurum Press|location=London|isbn=1854106252|pages=537–538}}</ref> The first floor features three-brick plat bands, while the second floor has a stepped cornice with windows under timber lintels.<ref name=":0" /> The building's doorways (one per face) and windows (one per face on the first and second floors) are all bricked in, a change that happened at an unknown time.<ref name="Headley" /> The name "The Pepperbox" came about due to the tower's resemblance to a [[pepper shaker|pepper pot]] or [[pepper box]],<ref name="Quinn">{{cite book|last1=Quinn|first1=Tom|title=Hidden Britain|date=29 August 2008|publisher=New Holland Publishers|location=Cape Town|isbn=978-1847731296|page=33|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sbfms1oJn8MC&q=pepper+box+wiltshire&pg=PA33|access-date=22 March 2018}}</ref> used in the 17th and 18th centuries,<ref name="Alderbury">{{cite book|last1=Alderbury and Whaddon Local History Research Group|title=Alderbury and Whaddon: a Millennium Mosaic of People, Places and Progress|date=2000|publisher=Alderbury & Whaddon Local History Research |isbn=0-9538004-0-7}}</ref> and consequently also inspired the name of the hill that it stands on.<ref name="Whitelaw" /> The tower bears some similarities with the influential, octagonal [[Tower of the Winds]] in [[Athens]], [[Greece]], as does the 1782 [[Mount Stewart#Temple of the Winds|folly of the same name]] at [[Mount Stewart]], although the Pepperbox predates Nicholas Revett and James Stuart's recording of the Athens tower by some 150 years.<ref name="Headley" />

The folly stands at the high point of the chalk ridge south-east of the city of [[Salisbury]], Wiltshire.<ref name="NT">{{Cite web|title=Pepperbox Hill|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/pepperbox-hill|access-date=2021-01-03|website=National Trust|language=en}}</ref> The highest point of Pepperbox Hill is further along the ridge to the north-west, where there is an [[Ordnance Survey]] [[Triangulation station|triangulation pillar]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Mountain Search|url=http://www.hill-bagging.co.uk/mountaindetails.php?qu=S&rf=18489|access-date=2021-12-07|website=www.hill-bagging.co.uk}}</ref> The site is in the north-west corner of the parish of [[Whiteparish]],<ref name="Wiltshire" /><ref name="Alderbury">{{cite book|last1=Alderbury and Whaddon Local History Research Group|title=Alderbury and Whaddon: a Millennium Mosaic of People, Places and Progress|date=2000|publisher=Alderbury & Whaddon Local History Research |isbn=0-9538004-0-7}}</ref> but is more closely associated with the village of [[Alderbury]], which the tower overlooks.<ref name="Wiltshire" /><ref name="Alderbury" /> The hill has far-reaching views both east and west,<ref name="Quinn" /> including over Salisbury.<ref name="Whitelaw">{{cite book|last1=Whitelaw|first1=Jeffrey W.|title=Follies|date=1 March 2005|publisher=Shire Books|location=London|isbn=0747806241|page=7|edition=3rd}}</ref> Gwen Headley suggests that the tower was built in the open countryside at such a location because Eyre believed that the land which the hill overlooks would "last forever," and that this potential impetus has been obscured by the changing of the landscape in the subsequent centuries.<ref name="Headley" /> The folly is surrounded by a diverse habitat boasting many uncommon species including [[juniper]], [[orchid]]s and [[yew]] woodland.<ref name="NT" />

==Later history==
In the early 18th century, the Pepperbox was allegedly used as a haunt by [[highwaymen]], who would attack carriages as they reached the summit of the hill, when the horses would be tired by the climb.<ref name="Quinn" /> The tower was used as a lookout post by the local [[Home Guard (United Kingdom)|Home Guard]] during World War II.<ref name="Wiltshire" /> It was designated a [[Grade II listed building]] as "The Pepperbox" in 1960,<ref name=":0" /> and today, both the folly and the hill it stands on are property of the [[National Trust]].<ref name="NT" />

In August and September 1990 a series of [[Free party|free parties]] were held next to the Pepperbox. These parties were organised by a loose anarchist collective who became known as the People From Pepperbox, or PFP. The Pepperbox parties are generally regarded as the first of their kind, where the concepts of [[Rave|raves]] and free festivals combined, becoming known as free parties.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Harrison |first=Harry |url= |title=Dreaming in yellow: the story of DiY Sound System |date=2022 |isbn=978-1-913231-14-9 |location=Bristol |page=104 |oclc=1295100308}}</ref>  

=== Assessment ===
Despite the theory that the Pepperbox was used as a lookout tower, it is today considered one of the earliest [[folly|follies]], dating from before the term "folly" was first used.<ref name="Whitelaw" /><ref name="Meulenkamp" /> The Pepperbox and the three other follies in and around Salisbury are regarded as the four oldest follies in Wiltshire.<ref name="Meulenkamp" /> Regarding the Pepperbox, Headley writes that due to the tower being "isolated, unprotected, enigmatic and blank," the sudden sight of the "strange, anonymous small building" provokes questions from unfamiliar passers-by. She notes that the tower is considered a folly because it is a "misunderstood building."<ref name="Headley" /> In their 1976 volume on Wiltshire in the ''Buildings of England'' series, [[Nikolaus Pevsner]] and Bridget Cherry note the Pepperbox as one of several early 17th century "oddments" in the county, alongside the two triangular [[gatehouse]]s of [[Amesbury]], built in 1600 and 1607, and Newhouse in [[Redlynch, Wiltshire|Redlynch]], built in 1619.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Pevsner|first1=Nikolaus|last2=Cherry|first2=Bridget|title=Wiltshire|date=27 May 1976|publisher=Penguin Books|location=London|isbn=0140710264|page=40|edition=2nd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Dk_moRw2Q7cC&q=eyre%27s+folly&pg=PA40|access-date=22 March 2018}}</ref> The Pepperbox is listed in Peter Long's book ''The Hidden Places of England''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Long|first1=Peter|title=The Hidden Places of England|date=March 2004|publisher=Travel Publishing|location=Berkshire|isbn=1904434126|page=577|edition=4th|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4ePshlzYVkAC&q=eyre%27s+folly&pg=PT582|access-date=22 March 2018}}</ref>
